options: Surgical drapes conceal the patient's face and airway, hiding accidental tube dislodgement or traction
Head flexion increases apparatus dead space beyond the capacity of the Y-piece
Electrosurgical units generate radiofrequencies that loosen corrugated plastic connectors
Nitrous oxide diffusion softens the 15 mm endotracheal tube adapter
questions.explanation: During head and neck surgery, surgical drapes cover the face and endotracheal tube. Movement of the surgical team or table manipulation can easily dislodge the circuit unseen beneath the drapes.

questions.stem: What type of fire extinguisher is specifically recommended for extinguishing a fire in the operating room when water or saline has failed?
options: Carbon dioxide (CO2) extinguisher
Dry chemical ammonium phosphate extinguisher
Pressurized foam extinguisher
Halon 1211 liquid agent extinguisher
questions.explanation: A carbon dioxide (CO2) fire extinguisher is recommended in the operating room because it leaves no corrosive chemical residue on patient tissues or delicate electronics.

questions.stem: What is the primary electrical hazard of using an electrosurgical unit (ESU / Bovie) on a patient with a permanent cardiac pacemaker?
options: High radiofrequency current can cause electrical interference, resulting in pacemaker reprogramming, inhibition, or myocardial burns at the lead tip
The ESU current causes instantaneous battery explosion within the pacemaker generator
The pacemaker ground wire diverts current, causing the line isolation monitor to trip
Radiofrequency current converts pacemaker pacing spikes into direct current shocks
questions.explanation: The high-frequency energy of an ESU interferes with cardiac pacemakers, potentially causing oversensing (inhibition of pacing), asynchronous resetting, damage to the internal circuitry, or myocardial burns where the lead meets the myocardium.

questions.stem: Agent dosage errors are rare with modern equipment. Which practice does the lecture say increases the risk?
options: Filling vaporizers with the key fill system
Keeping vaporizers mounted on one machine
Frequently moving vaporizers between machines
Using only one vaporizer at a time
questions.explanation: Dosage and administration errors (liquid agent in fresh gas piping, dial design, incorrect filling, simultaneous vaporizers) are rare, largely because equipment is well designed. The risk rises when vaporizers are moved frequently, since a tipped vaporizer can increase the dose.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 24 (PDF p. 12)

questions.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient is transported on a Mapleson C. Compared with controlled ventilation on the same circuit, what is the added problem?
options: The APL must be closed
The patient does more work of breathing to overcome rebreathing
FGF requirements fall to 0.7 x MV
The patient can't rebreathe during spontaneous breathing
questions.explanation: Mapleson B and C always permit rebreathing. To prevent hypercarbia, FGF of 1.5-2.5 x MV is used and the patient must hyperventilate; if spontaneously breathing, metabolic work increases. Controlled ventilation avoids that because the patient isn't doing the work. Instructor note: spontaneously breathing = Mapleson A.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which circle system arrangements must be avoided to prevent rebreathing? Select 3.
options: Reservoir bag between the patient and either unidirectional valve
Absorber in the inspiratory limb on the bag side
Fresh gas inlet between the patient and the expiratory valve
APL valve on the expiratory side near the bag
Fresh gas inlet on the inspiratory side downstream of the absorber
APL valve between the patient and the inspiratory valve
questions.explanation: The three arrangements to avoid: fresh gas inlet between patient and expiratory valve; APL between patient and inspiratory valve; reservoir bag between patient and either valve. The absorber in the inspiratory limb on the bag side is the standard placement.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: The lecture says grounding refers to two separate concepts that 'are not mutually exclusive.' What are they?
options: Grounding of electrical power and grounding of electrical equipment
Grounding of the patient and grounding of the provider
Grounding of AC and grounding of DC
Grounding of the ESU and grounding of the monitors
questions.explanation: Grounding applies to the power (grounded or ungrounded) and to the equipment (grounded or ungrounded). Power can energize devices that are themselves grounded or not. At home, power is grounded; in the OR, power is ungrounded while equipment is grounded.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 29 (PDF p. 15)

questions.stem: A technician removes the pins from an O2 hanger yoke so a cylinder with a damaged valve will fit. What is the main danger?
options: The cylinder can no longer form a gas-tight seal
A wrong-gas cylinder could be mounted, risking a hypoxic mixture
The first-stage regulator will pass full cylinder pressure
The yoke check valve will no longer seat properly
questions.explanation: PISS can be bypassed by removing the pins, which the lecture calls out as not recommended because it could result in hypoxic gas mixtures. The pins are what stop a wrong cylinder from fitting.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: How do electronically controlled flow controllers vary gas flow?
options: A bimetallic strip adjusts the orifice
A needle valve is turned by hand
A glass tube and float measure the flow
A variable-position solenoid sets the orifice size
questions.explanation: Electronic flow controllers are still variable-orifice devices, but the orifice size is controlled by a variable-position solenoid, with settings made through a computer interface on the workstation.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 12 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: After intubation, breath sounds and ETCO2 were confirmed. Ten minutes later, ETCO2 has risen steadily, there's no chest rise, and the bag hangs empty. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Exhausted CO2 absorbent
Increased apparatus dead space
An incompetent expiratory valve
The ventilator was never turned on
questions.explanation: The lecture's most common hypercarbia cause: intubating, confirming breath sounds and ETCO2, then forgetting to turn the ventilator on, so the patient isn't breathing. No chest rise with rising CO2 points to apnea, not rebreathing.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: A cylinder valve has a single pin-index hole in position 7. Which gas does the lecture's chart assign to it?
options: Medical air
Nitrous oxide
Carbon dioxide
Entonox
questions.explanation: From the PISS chart: oxygen 2,5; nitrous oxide 3,5; air 1,5; carbon dioxide 1,6; Entonox (50% N2O / 50% O2) uses the single position 7.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: What does impedance (Z) include that simple resistance doesn't?
options: Voltage and current
Power and energy
Only resistance at high voltage
Capacitance and inductance
questions.explanation: Impedance is the sum of the forces opposing electron movement in an AC circuit: resistance plus capacitance and inductance. For AC circuits, Ohm's law becomes E = I x Z.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 27 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: A cylinder valve has pin-index holes at positions 1 and 6. Per the lecture's PISS chart, which gas does it hold?
options: Entonox
Medical air
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: The chart on slide 7: oxygen 2,5; nitrous oxide 3,5; air 1,5; carbon dioxide 1,6; Entonox 7. Air shares position 1 but pairs it with 5.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: After induction, the patient is breathing spontaneously, and circuit pressure keeps climbing with each breath. What is the most common cause according to the lecture?
options: The absorbent is exhausted
The ventilator is running at too high a rate
The O2 flowmeter is off
The APL valve was left closed after induction
questions.explanation: High breathing-system pressure during spontaneous ventilation can come from an APL that's partly or fully closed (often left closed after induction), kinked tubing to the scavenging interface, or a failed interface positive-pressure relief valve.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 23 (PDF p. 12)

questions.stem: Which describe the anesthesia machine's main power supply, per the lecture? Select 2.
options: Radiofrequency current at 500 kHz
Ungrounded equipment chassis
Alternating current at 50-60 Hz
A battery that lasts about 8 hours
220-240 V direct current
questions.explanation: The power cord uses 90-130 V at 50-60 Hz alternating current. The backup battery lasts about 40 minutes (some 1-2 hours), radiofrequency is the ESU, and OR equipment is grounded.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 25 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: A fire starts on the patient's drapes. Which sequence matches the lecture's response?
options: Assess the patient, turn off gases, extinguish, remove drapes
Remove drapes, assess the patient, turn off gases, extinguish
Turn off gases, remove drapes and burning materials, extinguish, assess the patient
Extinguish, assess the patient, remove drapes, turn off gases
questions.explanation: Fire on the patient: turn off gases, remove drapes and burning materials, extinguish flames with water, saline, or an extinguisher, then assess the patient's status, devise a care plan, and assess for smoke inhalation.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 37 (PDF p. 19)

questions.stem: During an airway fire, the ETT is pulled and gases are stopped at the same moment. Which numbered elements of the fire triangle do these two actions remove?
options: Elements 2 and 3
Element 1 only
Elements 1 and 2
Element 2 only
questions.explanation: Element 2 is the oxidizer (O2, controlled by anesthesia), removed by stopping gases. Element 3 is fuel, and the lecture lists tracheal tubes as fuel, so pulling the tube removes it. Element 1 is the ignition source (the surgeon's cautery or laser).
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 33, 36 (PDF p. 17, 18)

questions.stem: Heliox and O2 are running, and N2O is then added. Why can the patient still receive a hypoxic mixture despite a working proportioning system?
options: The proportioning system only links N2O and O2, not other gases
The proportioning system shuts off when helium is detected
Helium blocks the fail-safe valve
The proportioning system only works below 2 L/min
questions.explanation: The proportioning system functions only between N2O and O2. With helium or air also flowing, O2 can be a small share of the total; the lecture's example is heliox plus N2O dropping O2 below 21%.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 14 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: In the OR fire triangle, which team member typically controls each element?
options: Ignition: anesthesia; oxidizer: surgeon; fuel: nursing
Ignition: nursing; oxidizer: anesthesia; fuel: surgeon
Ignition: surgeon; oxidizer: nursing; fuel: anesthesia
Ignition: surgeon; oxidizer: anesthesia; fuel: nursing
questions.explanation: The ignition source is almost always the surgeon's cautery, lasers, or light cords; the oxidizer is controlled by anesthesia through the ETT, mask, or cannula; and fuel (drapes, gauze, prep) is labeled nursing, though fuel is everywhere. Instructor note: oxidizer (anesthesia) + ignition (surgeon) + fuel (anything).
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 33 (PDF p. 17)

questions.stem: Two O2 cylinders hang on a double yoke, one at 1900 psig and one at 800 psig, both open. What is transfilling?
options: Gas flowing from the pipeline into the cylinders
Liquid N2O moving into the O2 cylinder
Gas flowing from the higher-pressure cylinder into the lower-pressure one
Gas flowing from the machine back out an empty yoke
questions.explanation: The lecture defines transfilling as gas flowing from a higher-pressure cylinder to a lower-pressure cylinder, which a double hanger yoke can allow. The unidirectional valve in each yoke limits leaking from an empty yoke and lets cylinders be changed during use.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 9 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: Which electrical items should the machine check and your own preparation confirm? Select 2.
options: That the ESU return pad is on the anesthesia machine
That the vaporizers are electrically powered
That the machine's power is grounded like a home outlet
The backup battery is charged
Which functions (monitors, alarms, ventilator) run on battery
That the battery lasts at least 8 hours
questions.explanation: Instructor notes: make sure the battery is charged (machine check) and know what is powered by the battery; monitors, airway monitors, BP and HR, alarms, and the ventilator may or may not all share the same power source.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 25 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: With a constant 16 psi at the flow control valve inlet, what happens when the needle valve is opened further?
options: Resistance rises, so flow decreases
Pressure rises, so flow increases
Flow stays constant, because inlet pressure is fixed
Resistance falls, so flow increases
questions.explanation: Flow = pressure / resistance. Opening the valve (turning left) enlarges the orifice and decreases resistance, so flow rises; the instructor notes 'Ohm's law can be proven true once again.'
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 5, 13 (PDF p. 3, 7)

questions.stem: During a closed-system (very low-flow) anesthetic, SpO2 slowly falls. The circuit has no leaks, and the O2 analyzer shows FiO2 steadily dropping. Which highlighted hazard fits?
options: Disconnected O2 hose at the wall outlet
Closed-system anesthesia with inadequate fresh O2 supply
Incompetent circuit unidirectional valves
Crossed hospital O2 and N2O pipelines upstream
questions.explanation: With very low flow, O2 added must at least match what the patient consumes; otherwise circuit O2 falls. That's a highlighted item on slide 19. Crossed pipelines would drop FiO2 regardless of flow, and a disconnected hose triggers supply alarms.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 19 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Which statements about current types are correct? Select 2.
options: DC is harmless because it flows in one direction
For DC circuits, Ohm's law is written E = I x Z
Impedance applies only to DC circuits
AC reverses direction at regular intervals
AC flows in one direction only
About three times as much DC as AC is needed to cause V-fib
questions.explanation: DC flows in one direction; AC reverses at regular intervals. It takes about three times as much DC as AC to cause V-fib, which doesn't make DC harmless. Impedance applies to AC, where E = I x Z.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 27 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: During neck surgery with the drape over the face, the low exhaled volume alarm sounds. What does the lecture say is especially common here?
options: Ventilator malfunction from a failed bellows
Disconnection at the ETT connection under the drape
Absorbent exhaustion from high fresh gas flow
Vaporizer tipping as the table is rotated
questions.explanation: Circuit leaks and disconnections are especially common with neck surgery when the drape covers the face and the ET tube connection comes loose.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 23 (PDF p. 12)

questions.stem: A fire isn't going out with initial measures. Which steps does the lecture list? Select 3.
options: Increase FiO2 to protect the patient
Continue the procedure until the fire department arrives
Use a CO2 fire extinguisher
Activate the fire alarm
Reopen the room door to check on the fire
Turn off the medical gas supply to the room
questions.explanation: Failure to extinguish: use a CO2 fire extinguisher, activate the fire alarm, consider evacuating the room (close the door and don't reopen it), and turn off the medical gas supply to the room.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 38 (PDF p. 19)

questions.stem: A cylinder regulator has an inlet gauge and an outlet gauge. Which one changes as the cylinder empties?
options: Both, equally
The outlet gauge
The inlet gauge
Neither, because the regulator holds both steady
questions.explanation: The regulator converts variable high-pressure input (0 to about 2200 psi) into a constant lower output (about 45 psi). The inlet gauge tracks cylinder pressure and falls as it empties; the outlet stays constant. This was the instructor's question on slide 10.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 10 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: Why can't an air pipeline hose be connected to the machine's O2 inlet?
options: The O2 inlet uses the pin-index system to reject air
The fail-safe valve blocks air from entering the O2 line
Each DISS fitting differs in nut size, thread, and internal inlet
Air and O2 hoses differ only in their color coding
questions.explanation: DISS gives each gas a different diameter inlet and threading; not only is the external nut differently sized and threaded, but internally the inlets are different and non-interchangeable. Color helps, but the physical fit prevents misconnection.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 6 (PDF p. 3)

questions.stem: On some older anesthesia machines, the O2 flow control knob can't be turned completely off. Why?
options: To guarantee a minimal O2 flow
To keep the fail-safe valve open
To allow the flush valve to work
To prevent needle valve damage
questions.explanation: In some older machines, O2 can't be completely turned off at the control knob, allowing a minimal O2 flow as a safety feature.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 12 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: A proposed common gas outlet adapter uses a 30 mm conical fitting. Why doesn't it meet workstation standards?
options: Only 15 mm external fittings are allowed
19 and 30 mm conical fittings are reserved for the scavenging system
The standard requires a 22 mm internal diameter
30 mm is too small for the breathing circuit
questions.explanation: The standard allows one common gas outlet with a 15 mm internal (female) diameter and a 22 mm external (male) diameter. It can't have a 19 or 30 mm conical fitting because those sizes are specific to scavenging, which prevents misconnection.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: On a double-yoke machine where both O2 cylinders share one gauge, one cylinder is empty and the other full. What does the gauge show?
options: The average of the two cylinder pressures
Only the empty cylinder's pressure, near zero
A single pressure that can't tell the two cylinders apart
Two separate pressures on a split dial face
questions.explanation: On a single-cylinder system the gauge is upstream of the check valve and shows that cylinder's pressure. In a two-cylinder system the shared gauge location means you can't differentiate the individual cylinder pressures.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: A mixture of 50% O2 and 50% N2O is used near an ignition source. How does the lecture rate its fire risk?
options: It suppresses combustion, since N2O isn't an oxidizer
It supports combustion about as avidly as 100% O2
It's no riskier than room air
It supports combustion about half as much as 100% O2
questions.explanation: O2 and N2O function equally well as oxidizers, so a 50% O2 / 50% N2O combination would support combustion about as avidly as 100% oxygen. That's why the prevention list says to avoid N2O.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 33 (PDF p. 17)

questions.stem: Circuits 2 and 3 in the figure share which feature?
options: Fresh gas enters near the patient; they need 1.5-2.5 x MV
Fresh gas enters at the bag, so they need only 0.7 x MV
They're designed for spontaneous breathing only
They contain unidirectional valves and a CO2 absorber
questions.explanation: Circuits 2 and 3 are Mapleson B and C: fresh gas enters near the patient end, and exhaled gas is directed into a blind pouch, so they always permit rebreathing and need FGF of 1.5-2.5 x MV. Controlled ventilation avoids the extra work for a spontaneously breathing patient.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: A long elbow extension is added between the Y-piece and the ETT for positioning. ETCO2 slowly rises. What is the mechanism?
options: Increased apparatus dead space
Circuit leak
Incompetent unidirectional valves
Exhausted absorbent
questions.explanation: Tubing extensions between the Y-piece and patient add apparatus dead space, a delivery-system cause of hypercarbia on slide 20. Exhausted absorbent and bad valves cause rebreathing through the circle; a leak lowers exhaled volume.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Which pair of figures does the lecture give for gas delivery equipment problems?
options: 15 of about 6,000 claims; event incidence estimated at 0.02%
115 of about 60,000 claims; event incidence estimated at 2-4%
1,150 of about 6,000 claims; event incidence estimated at 19%
115 of about 6,000 closed claims; event incidence estimated at 0.23-0.4%
questions.explanation: The ASA closed claims database recorded 115 cases related to gas delivery equipment out of roughly 6,000 claims, and the incidence of such events has been estimated at 0.23-0.4%. Most adverse events are multifactorial, with human error responsible for the majority.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 17 (PDF p. 9)
questions.disc: The lecture audio links the two numbers ('115 of about 6,000, about 0.23-0.4%'), but 115 of 6,000 is about 1.9% of claims. The written notes present 0.23-0.4% as the estimated event incidence, a separate figure.

questions.stem: Which are the early warning signs of a surgical fire listed in the lecture? Select 3.
options: A fall in SpO2
A sudden rise in ETCO2
A rise in peak airway pressure
A pop
A flash
Smoke
questions.explanation: Look for early warning signs of fire: a pop, a flash, or smoke. Then stop the procedure, and each team member immediately carries out their assigned task. The monitor changes listed aren't the lecture's fire warning signs.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 36 (PDF p. 18)

questions.stem: Why is the O2 flow control knob larger in diameter with bigger ridges than the N2O and air knobs?
options: To meet DISS requirements
To allow a tactile safety check in addition to color
To make O2 flow easier to fine-tune
To withstand higher O2 pipeline pressure
questions.explanation: Knobs are color coded (O2 green in the US) and touch coded, so a provider gets both a visual and a tactile check. The instructor's aviation comparison: someone somewhere once gave a hypoxic mixture by turning the wrong knob.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 13 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: How does the current needed to cause ventricular fibrillation compare between DC and AC?
options: About three times more AC than DC is needed
They're equal
About three times more DC than AC is needed
DC can't cause ventricular fibrillation
questions.explanation: It takes about three times as much DC as AC to cause V-fib, but that doesn't make DC harmless. AC reverses direction at regular intervals, and AC circuits add impedance (E = I x Z).
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 27 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: An alcohol-based skin prep has pooled under the patient's flank just before draping. What is the correct action?
options: Use cautery on the lowest setting
Drape immediately so the prep stays sterile
Let the prep dry fully before draping and using cautery
Cover the pool with a dry towel and proceed
questions.explanation: Flammable prep solutions such as alcohol and acetone can ignite when the ESU is used. The lecture's prevention list starts with allowing flammable skin preparations to dry before draping.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 31, 35 (PDF p. 16, 18)

questions.stem: A Mapleson C is used with a minute ventilation of 5 L/min. What fresh gas flow range does the lecture recommend to prevent rebreathing?
options: 3.5-5 L/min
5-7.5 L/min
questions.explanation: Mapleson B and C always permit rebreathing through their blind-pouch design and need FGF of 1.5-2.5 x minute ventilation: 1.5 x 5 = 7.5 and 2.5 x 5 = 12.5 L/min. 3.5 L/min is the 0.7 x MV Mapleson A value.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Per the lecture audio, which aggravating factors are becoming increasingly common causes of adverse events?
options: Equipment failures from aging anesthesia machines
Inattention and distraction, often from phones or conversation
Inexperience among senior, long-practicing providers
Failure of hospital pipeline supply systems
questions.explanation: Inattention and distraction are increasingly common causes, often from phone use or getting pulled into conversation with the surgical team. Haste is another major factor, and fatigue affects nearly everyone.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 18 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: On these unlabeled valves, which numbered valve has the pin-index holes that fit a nitrous oxide yoke (positions 3 and 5)?
options: Valve 1
Valve 2
Valve 3
Valve 4
questions.explanation: Positions 3 and 5 are adjacent, so the N2O valve has its two holes close together, as on valve 2. O2 (2,5), air (1,5), and CO2 (1,6) have holes spaced farther apart.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: Total power is lost and the battery is exhausted. Which vaporizers can still deliver agent? Select 2.
options: GE Aladin desflurane cassette
GE Aladin sevoflurane cassette
Variable bypass sevoflurane vaporizer
Tec 6 desflurane vaporizer
Drager D-Vapor desflurane vaporizer
Variable bypass isoflurane vaporizer
questions.explanation: Once the battery is exhausted, only basic functions remain, including emergency O2 usable with a conventional mechanical (variable bypass) vaporizer. Desflurane vaporizers (Tec 6, D-Vapor) and electronic vaporizers like the GE Aladin can't deliver agent without electrical power.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 32 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: How many common gas outlets does the anesthesia workstation standard allow?
options: One per vaporizer
One
Two, one for each breathing system
As many as the manufacturer chooses
questions.explanation: The standard requires only one common gas outlet, with a 15 mm internal and 22 mm external diameter; 19 and 30 mm conical fittings are reserved for scavenging.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: Which are HYPERCARBIA hazards on the lecture's delivery-system list (as opposed to hypoxemia hazards)? Select 3.
options: Exhausted CO2 absorbent or channeling
Crossed hospital pipelines
Closed O2 cylinder valve
O2 flowmeter turned off
Increased apparatus dead space
Incorrectly assembled circle system
questions.explanation: Hypercarbia hazards: apnea, increased apparatus dead space, missing or incompetent unidirectional valves, incorrectly assembled circle, exhausted absorbent or channeling, and inadequate FGF without absorption. A closed O2 cylinder, crossed pipelines, and a flowmeter left off are hypoxemia hazards on slide 19.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 19, 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Running behind schedule, a new provider extubates a patient who isn't adequately awake. Which aggravating factor from the lecture does this illustrate?
options: Failure to check equipment
Fatigue
Haste
Lack of familiarity with equipment
questions.explanation: The instructor's example of haste is exactly this: time pressure, especially early in a career, leading to errors like extubating before a patient is adequately awake. The other listed factors are failure to check equipment, unfamiliarity, inexperience, inattention, distraction, and fatigue.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 18 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: A device draws 10 A from a 120 V source. Using Ohm's law, what is its resistance?
options: 1.2 ohms
12 ohms
130 ohms
1,200 ohms
questions.explanation: E = I x R, so R = E / I = 120 V / 10 A = 12 ohms. 1,200 would come from multiplying instead of dividing.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 26 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: Which are IGNITION sources in the OR, per the lecture? Select 3.
options: Nitrous oxide in the circuit
Paper surgical drapes
Lasers
Electrosurgical unit
Oxygen at high FiO2
Ends of fiberoptic light cords
questions.explanation: Ignition sources: the ESU, lasers, and the ends of fiberoptic light cords. O2 and N2O are oxidizers, and drapes are fuel.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 33 (PDF p. 17)

questions.stem: On an older machine with a chain linking the O2 and N2O valves, O2 is turned down below 25% of total flow. What happens?
options: N2O flow decreases too
O2 flow is automatically raised to 50%
An alarm sounds but flows are unchanged
The fail-safe valve closes
questions.explanation: In older machines, the linkage was a mechanical chain between the O2 and N2O valves (14 and 28 teeth on the gears). If O2 is turned below 25% of total flow, N2O flow decreases as well. Modern machines do this electronically.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 14 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: During a power failure, about how long does a typical anesthesia machine backup battery last?
options: About 40 minutes
Indefinitely, while alarms are muted
About 5 minutes
About 8 hours
questions.explanation: The backup battery usually provides power for approximately 40 minutes (some machines 1-2 hours). Know exactly what runs on battery alone (monitors, alarms, ventilator), and confirm it's charged on the machine check.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 25 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: The morning machine check was delegated to an anesthesia tech. What does the lecture advise before starting the first case?
options: Skip it, since delegation makes it the tech's responsibility
Check only the O2 cylinder pressure
Confirm the check was actually completed
Repeat only the vaporizer check
questions.explanation: Most hypoxemia hazards trace back to an incomplete or skipped machine check. The lecture says to confirm the morning check was actually completed, especially when it's delegated to a tech.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 19 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: In the lecture's analogy between Ohm's law (E = I x R) and hemodynamics (BP = CO x SVR), which pairing is correct?
options: Voltage = BP; current = SVR; resistance = cardiac output
Voltage = SVR; current = cardiac output; resistance = BP
Voltage = cardiac output; current = BP; resistance = SVR
Voltage = BP; current = cardiac output; resistance = SVR
questions.explanation: E = I x R maps onto BP = CO x SVR: voltage corresponds to blood pressure, current to cardiac output, and resistance to systemic vascular resistance.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 26 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: On this slide, the highlighted hypoxemia hazards share what feature, according to the instructor's notes?
options: They're usually picked up on the machine check
They can only be detected by pulse oximetry
They're all caused by pipeline failures
They all originate upstream of the workstation
questions.explanation: The instructor's note: highlighted things are usually picked up on the machine check (crossed hoses, disconnected hose, failed backup O2, empty or closed cylinder, bad valves, circuit leak, inadequate fresh O2, inadequate ventilation). The upstream items (liquid reservoir, crossed hospital pipelines, closed pipeline valves) aren't highlighted.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 19 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Mid-case, the machine switches to battery after a building power failure. What is the best use of the battery window?
options: Wait for the low-battery alarm before changing anything
Turn off the monitors to save battery for the ventilator
Switch to desflurane, since it's independent of power
Set up a Mapleson for ventilation and a TIVA infusion now
questions.explanation: The battery buys roughly 40 minutes to 2 hours. The lecture says to use that window to set up alternatives, like a Mapleson for ventilation and an IV infusion such as propofol, so the patient is safely covered well before the battery runs out (generally within about an hour). Des vaporizers need power.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 25, 32 (PDF p. 13, 16)

questions.stem: Which hypoxemia hazards originate upstream of the workstation? Select 3.
options: Closed pipeline valves
Disconnected O2 hose in the OR
Incompetent circuit unidirectional valves
Liquid O2 reservoir empty or filled with nitrogen
Crossed hospital pipelines
Empty O2 cylinder on the machine
questions.explanation: The slide lists these under 'upstream of the workstation': the liquid O2 reservoir, crossed hospital pipelines, and closed pipeline valves. An empty machine cylinder, a disconnected OR hose, and incompetent valves are at the workstation or circuit (and are among the highlighted items a machine check usually catches).
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 19 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: After a case using an isolated ESU, the patient has a burn under the return pad, which had partly lifted. What explains this?
options: The pad was placed too close to the surgical site
The isolated ESU leaked standard 60 Hz current to the pad
The ECG pads were placed too close to the return pad
Poor pad contact concentrated the current; isolation doesn't prevent it
questions.explanation: The return electrode disperses current over a large area. If the pad doesn't make proper contact, current concentrates and can burn. Although the isolated ESU adds safety, it's no foolproof protection against burns from an improperly applied pad. Placing the pad close to the site is recommended.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: A device draws 5 A at 120 V for 10 seconds. How much energy does it use?
options: 60 joules
600 joules
6,000 joules
60,000 joules
questions.explanation: Power P = E x I = 120 V x 5 A = 600 watts. Energy = watts x seconds = 600 x 10 = 6,000 joules (watt-seconds), the same unit used for defibrillator output. 600 is the power in watts, not the energy.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 26 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient on a Mapleson A has a minute ventilation of 6 L/min. What is the minimum fresh gas flow per the lecture?
options: About 2 L/min
About 4.2 L/min
About 9 L/min
About 15 L/min
questions.explanation: Mapleson A (Magill) is used with spontaneously breathing patients and needs FGF of at least 0.7 x minute ventilation: 0.7 x 6 = 4.2 L/min. 9-15 L/min is the 1.5-2.5 x MV range for Mapleson B and C.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Why is pipeline O2 pressure (50-55 psi) deliberately set higher than the cylinder regulator output (40-45 psi)?
options: So the machine draws from the pipeline and keeps the cylinder in reserve
So the fail-safe can sense which source is in use
So both sources mix to keep flow constant
So the cylinder supplies the machine and the pipeline stays in reserve
questions.explanation: The difference is deliberate: when both are connected, gas is preferentially drawn from the pipeline, leaving the cylinder as backup. That's also why the pipeline must be disconnected to use the cylinder when the pipeline supply is contaminated.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 2)

questions.stem: During spontaneous ventilation, circuit pressure rises even though the APL is fully open. What else does the lecture list as a cause?
options: Kinked tubing between the APL and scavenging interface
A disconnected O2 hose
An open negative-pressure relief valve
High fresh gas flow with an open APL
questions.explanation: High pressure during spontaneous ventilation can come from APL closure, kinking or occlusion of the tubing between the APL and scavenging interface, or malfunction of the interface's positive-pressure relief valve. Gas that can't leave through the APL backs up into the circuit.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 23 (PDF p. 12)

questions.stem: An airway fire flashes in the ETT. What does current teaching say about removing the tube and stopping gas flow?
options: Stop gases first, then remove the tube
Pour saline first, then decide
Do both simultaneously
Remove the tube first, then stop gases
questions.explanation: For an airway fire: simultaneously remove the tracheal tube and stop gases or disconnect the circuit, pour saline into the airway, remove burning material, then mask ventilate, assess injury, consider bronchoscopy, and reintubate.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 36 (PDF p. 18)

questions.stem: On an older field machine, a freestanding PEEP valve is attached in the wrong position. Where does the lecture say it can cause obstruction?
options: In the inspiratory limb of a circle system
At the scavenging interface
In the expiratory limb of a circle system
At the common gas outlet
questions.explanation: A freestanding PEEP valve may cause obstruction if it's incorrectly placed in the inspiratory limb. These valves are rarely used now since PEEP is built into most machines.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 22 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which are fire PREPARATION steps, as opposed to response or aftermath steps? Select 3.
options: Pour saline into the airway
Assign each person a task in advance
Practice responses with fire drills
Preserve the scene for the risk manager
Train personnel in OR fire management
Turn off the medical gas supply to the room
questions.explanation: Preparation: train personnel, practice fire drills, ensure equipment is available, identify high-risk situations, decide how to prevent and manage a fire, and assign each person a task. Turning off room gases is a failure-to-extinguish step, saline in the airway is airway fire management, and preserving the scene comes after.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 34, 36, 38, 39 (PDF p. 17, 18, 19, 20)

questions.stem: A defibrillator delivers 200 joules. How is that energy expressed in the lecture's terms?
options: 200 watt-seconds
200 volts
200 amperes
200 ohms
questions.explanation: Power (watts) = voltage x current, and electrical work = watts x time. The watt-second (joule) is the unit for energy expended, which is how defibrillator discharge is measured.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 26 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: Which of these are aggravating factors in anesthesia adverse events, per the lecture? Select 3.
options: Lack of familiarity with equipment
Routine fire drills
Failure to check equipment
Redundant alarm systems
Inattention
Standardized connector sizes
questions.explanation: The listed aggravating factors: failure to check equipment, lack of familiarity with equipment, inexperience, haste, inattention, distraction, and fatigue. Standardized connectors, redundant alarms, and fire drills are protective measures.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 18 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: During a prolonged power failure, why does the machine cut all power when battery voltage falls below about 10 V?
options: To prevent deep discharge of the battery
To protect the O2 fail-safe valve
To force the ventilator into manual mode
To reset the circuit breakers
questions.explanation: When battery voltage drops below about 10 V, all power to the machine ceases to prevent deep discharge. Failure of the battery stops the monitors, alarms, and ventilator, so plan an alternative well before that point.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 25 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: A machine has two flowmeter tubes for O2 connected in series. What is the purpose of the first tube?
options: Measurement of high flows only
Calibration of the second tube
Accurate measurement of low flows
A backup if the second tube cracks
questions.explanation: When two flowmeters are present, the first permits accurate measurement of low flows and the second measures higher flows. The Thorpe tube is tapered, narrower at the bottom, with a ball or bobbin float.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 12 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: ESU current (500 kHz to 1 MHz) can pass across the precordium. Why doesn't it cause ventricular fibrillation?
options: OR power is ungrounded, which blocks cardiac current
Its high frequency has low tissue penetration and doesn't excite heart cells
The return pad blocks the current from reaching the chest
The ESU uses DC, which needs three times more current
questions.explanation: The ESU generates radiofrequency current that behaves differently from standard 60 Hz AC: it has low tissue penetration and doesn't excite contractile cells, so it can pass through the precordium without causing V-fib.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient needs transport, and you plan FGF of 0.7 x minute ventilation. Which numbered circuit is appropriate?
options: Circuit 1
Circuit 2
Circuit 3
Any of the three at that flow
questions.explanation: Circuit 1 is the Mapleson A (Magill): fresh gas enters at the bag end, with the relief valve near the patient. It's the circuit for spontaneous breathing and needs FGF of at least 0.7 x MV. Circuits 2 and 3 are Mapleson B and C, which need 1.5-2.5 x MV.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which belong in an OR's contingency plan for a prolonged power failure during a desflurane anesthetic? Select 3.
options: A Mapleson system for ventilation
Waiting for the low-battery alarm before acting
Relying on the Tec 6 vaporizer while on battery
Having the plan in place well before the battery runs out
Switching to an Aladin cassette for agent delivery
An IV anesthetic infusion such as propofol
questions.explanation: Every OR needs a contingency plan. Use the battery window to set up a Mapleson for ventilation and a TIVA infusion, and have the patient covered well before the battery is gone (generally within about an hour). The Tec 6 and Aladin both depend on electrical power.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 32 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: These cylinder valves are shown with their gas labels removed. Which numbered valve belongs to an Entonox cylinder?
options: Valve 1
Valve 3
Valve 4
Valve 5
questions.explanation: Entonox uses a single pin-index position (7), and valve 5 is the only one with a single hole. The two-hole valves are O2 (2,5), N2O (3,5), air (1,5), and CO2 (1,6).
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: Which statements about adverse events in anesthesia practice match the lecture? Select 2.
options: Most are multifactorial
Human error is responsible for the majority
Most are caused by isolated equipment failures
Most involve a single root cause
Most occur only during induction
Equipment problems are too rare to matter
questions.explanation: Most adverse events are multifactorial, combining system problems, human factors, and technical failures, and human error is responsible for the majority. The instructor stressed that low incidence doesn't mean equipment issues are safe to ignore.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 17 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: Why does a machine need a proportioning system in addition to the O2 fail-safe valve?
options: It doesn't function at all on modern electronic machines
It measures inspired O2, which responds too slowly
It only cuts N2O when O2 pressure falls; it can't stop a bad flow ratio
It only works while the machine runs on cylinder O2
questions.explanation: The pressure-sensor shut-off (fail-safe) only interrupts or reduces N2O when O2 pressure falls; it doesn't prevent a hypoxic mixture reaching the common gas outlet when O2 pressure is normal but flow settings are wrong. The proportioning system addresses the flow ratio.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 14 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: Which hypercarbia hazard applies to a system WITHOUT carbon dioxide absorption?
options: Absorbent desiccation
Inadequate fresh gas flow
Channeling in the canister
Exhausted absorbent
questions.explanation: In a system without CO2 absorption, fresh gas flow is what clears CO2, so inadequate FGF causes rebreathing. Exhausted absorbent and channeling are hazards of systems WITH an absorber.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: What protects the machine's AC power supply, battery, and convenience receptacles?
options: The ESU return pad
Circuit breakers
The backup battery
The line isolation monitor
questions.explanation: The workstation's electrical portion has several circuit breakers, which generally protect circuits for the AC supply, the battery, and the convenience receptacles. The power cord runs 90-130 V AC at 50-60 Hz.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 25 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: Which sequence matches the lecture's risk management steps?
options: Define problems, estimate likelihood, weigh resources, apply solutions, monitor
Monitor, define problems, weigh resources, apply solutions, estimate likelihood
Estimate likelihood, apply solutions, define problems, monitor, weigh resources
Apply solutions, define problems, monitor, estimate likelihood, weigh resources
questions.explanation: Risk management: define potential problems, estimate the likelihood of occurrence, weigh the benefits of expending available resources, apply solutions, and monitor.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 16 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: After the machine check, the O2 cylinder is left open. At 2 a.m., the pipeline fails during an emergency case. When does the O2 supply alarm sound?
options: Immediately when pipeline pressure starts to fall
Only after the cylinder has quietly emptied
Never, because the cylinder takes over permanently
When the fail-safe valve closes the N2O line
questions.explanation: With the cylinder open, the machine starts drawing from it as soon as pipeline pressure drops, so supply pressure stays up and no alarm sounds until the cylinder is empty. That's why the cylinder should be closed after checking it: the alarm then warns you at the pipeline failure while a full backup is still available.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 2)

questions.stem: A circle system is assembled with the fresh gas inlet between the patient and the expiratory unidirectional valve. What is the problem?
options: The APL can no longer vent
Fresh gas bypasses the patient, promoting rebreathing
The absorber is bypassed entirely
Fresh gas pressure closes the inspiratory valve
questions.explanation: The circle must be arranged to prevent rebreathing, and three arrangements must be avoided: fresh gas inlet between the patient and expiratory valve, APL between the patient and inspiratory valve, and reservoir bag between the patient and either valve. Misplacing the inlet sends fresh gas out the expiratory side instead of to the patient.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: After the workstation battery is fully exhausted, which functions remain available?
options: The ventilator and monitors on reduced power
Nothing; all O2 delivery stops
Emergency O2 and conventional mechanical vaporizers
Electronic flow control and alarms
questions.explanation: Once the battery is exhausted, only basic functions remain: emergency oxygen, which can be used with a conventional variable bypass vaporizer. The ventilator, monitors, and alarms are lost.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 32 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: A machine has an outlet check valve. How must the low-pressure system be tested for leaks?
options: With the O2 flush while occluding the Y-piece
It can't be tested for leaks
With positive pressure at the common gas outlet
With negative pressure
questions.explanation: Without a check valve, low-pressure leaks can be found by applying positive pressure at the common gas outlet. With a check valve, positive pressure can't reach the upstream components, so negative pressure must be applied.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: Which agent-delivery hazard does the lecture list along with dial design and incorrect filling?
options: Low O2 supply pressure at the inlet
Crossed pipeline supply hoses
Exhausted CO2 absorbent granules
Liquid agent in the fresh gas piping
questions.explanation: Anesthetic agent dosage and administration problems: liquid agent in the fresh gas piping, concentration dial design, incorrect filling, and simultaneous use of more than one vaporizer. Tipping a vaporizer can put liquid where it doesn't belong.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 24 (PDF p. 12)

questions.stem: Which are functions of the cylinder hanger yoke? Select 3.
options: Ensures unidirectional flow into the machine
Links O2 and N2O flows
Reduces cylinder pressure to about 45 psi
Orients the cylinder
Provides a gas-tight seal
Displays the cylinder's remaining volume
questions.explanation: The hanger yoke orients the cylinder, provides a gas-tight seal, and ensures unidirectional flow into the machine; it also contains a filter. Reducing pressure is the regulator's job just distal to the yoke, the gauge shows pressure, and the proportioning system links O2 and N2O.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 9 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: The machine check keeps failing the leak test, and no single loose component can be found. Per the instructor's notes, what usually fixes it?
options: Recalibrating the O2 analyzer
Replacing the scavenging interface
Replacing the O2 cylinder
Swapping the breathing circuit
questions.explanation: Breathing circuit leaks are a common failure point, and the note says swapping the circuit usually fixes a failed leak check. Circuit leaks are one of the highlighted hypoxemia hazards usually caught on the machine check.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 19 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Which components are part of the lecture's definition of the anesthesia workstation? Select 3.
options: Wall suction regulator
Anesthetic gas scavenging system
Gas delivery system
Operating room ventilation system
Hospital bulk liquid O2 tank
Anesthesia ventilator
questions.explanation: The workstation is defined as the gas delivery system, breathing system, scavenging system, vapor delivery system, ventilator, and associated monitoring and protection devices. The bulk O2 tank and OR ventilation are facility systems upstream of or around the workstation.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 2 (PDF p. 1)

questions.stem: Why does the lecture say risk management is especially difficult in anesthesia?
options: Equipment failures cause the majority of adverse events
Complications are frequent enough to overwhelm reporting
Complications only occur inside the operating room
Complications are rare, so providers get little practice responding
questions.explanation: The difficulty is the rarity of events: it's hard to develop solutions for events that rarely happen, and that rarity creates its own hazard because providers aren't experienced or trained to respond. Complications also aren't isolated to the OR; they can trace through pre-op, PACU, and the floor.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 16 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: A capacitor in a DC circuit is connected to a battery. What happens to current flow?
options: Only a momentary current flows while the plates charge
Current flows continuously through the insulator
Current reverses direction at regular intervals
No current flows at any time
questions.explanation: A capacitor is two parallel conductors separated by an insulator. In a DC circuit, the plates charge with only a momentary current flow; no further current flows unless a resistance connects the plates and discharges the capacitor.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 28 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: After an airway fire is controlled, a staff member starts throwing the burned ETT and circuit in the trash. What does the lecture say?
options: Keep only the ETT; the circuit can be discarded
Discard everything promptly to prevent a second fire
That's fine once photos of the scene are taken
Stop; preserve the scene, including tube, circuit, and drapes
questions.explanation: Risk management after a fire: preserve the scene, notify the hospital risk manager, follow reporting requirements, treat it as an adverse event, and run fire drills. Leave everything in place, including the ET tube, circuit, and pulled drapes.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 39 (PDF p. 20)

questions.stem: How does grounding in the operating room differ from grounding at home?
options: Both power and equipment are ungrounded in the OR
OR power is ungrounded while equipment is grounded
Both power and equipment are grounded in the OR
OR power is grounded while equipment is ungrounded
questions.explanation: At home, electrical power is grounded and equipment may or may not be. In the OR it's the opposite: power is usually ungrounded, and the equipment is grounded.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 29 (PDF p. 15)

questions.stem: Why is power supplied to most ORs ungrounded?
options: So OR equipment can run safely without being grounded
To isolate current from ground potential, protecting against macroshock
So the ESU can work without a dispersive return pad
To lower electrical costs for high-draw OR equipment
questions.explanation: With many devices, cords, and spilled fluids, the OR is an electrically hazardous environment. Ungrounded power isolates current from ground potential, an additional measure of protection from macroshock.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 30 (PDF p. 15)

questions.stem: Which items does the lecture list as reported causes of total occlusion of the breathing circuit?
options: An APL valve left fully open during ventilation
Loose vaporizer filler caps on the manifold
Filters, misconnected humidifiers, and defective tubing
Exhausted absorbent and channeling in the canister
questions.explanation: Filters in the circuit, incorrectly connected humidifiers, manufacturing defects in tubing, and failure to remove plastic wrapping have all been reported as causes of total breathing-circuit occlusion. Adapters also risk misconnections.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 22 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which statements about ESU safety match the lecture? Select 2.
options: ECG pads should be placed right next to the surgical site
ESU current is standard 60 Hz AC
An isolated ESU doesn't prevent pad-contact burns
Prep solutions don't need to dry before cautery
The return pad should be placed far from the surgical site
Unit won't work unless pencil and pad are both connected
questions.explanation: The ESU requires both the pencil and the return pad to be connected, which acts as a built-in safety check, but an isolated ESU is no foolproof protection against pad burns. Place the pad close to the site and ECG pads far away. ESU current is radiofrequency (500 kHz-1 MHz), and prep must dry first.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: In the cylinder regulator described in the lecture, how is output held at about 45 psi?
options: Two linked diaphragms use negative feedback to close the inlet
The fail-safe valve limits gas flow into the machine
A bimetallic strip responds to cylinder temperature
The provider adjusts a needle valve as pressure falls
questions.explanation: Immediately distal to the hanger yoke, two diaphragms are connected by a rod. Gas entering pushes on the large diaphragm, which moves the small one to close the high-pressure inlet, a negative feedback loop that holds about 45 psi.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 9 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: Which devices can the ESU's high-frequency energy interfere with, per the lecture? Select 3.
options: Pulse oximeters
The O2 fail-safe valve
ECG
The pipeline check valves
Variable bypass vaporizers
Implanted cardiac pacemakers
questions.explanation: Few things in the OR are immune to the Bovie: its high-frequency energy interferes with everything from the ECG signal to cardiac output computers, pulse oximeters, and implanted pacemakers. Pneumatic and mechanical components like the fail-safe, vaporizers, and check valves aren't affected.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: Where should the ESU return pad and the ECG electrodes be placed relative to the surgical site?
options: Both as far from the site as possible
Both close to the surgical site
Return pad far from the site; ECG pads close to it
Return pad close to the site; ECG pads as far away as feasible
questions.explanation: It's prudent to place the return plate as close as possible to the operative site, and ECG pads as far from the site as feasible, keeping the current path short and away from monitoring leads.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: Besides O2, N2O, and air, which pipeline connections on the lecture's DISS chart have their own gas-specific fittings? Select 2.
options: Waste anesthetic gas disposal (WAGD)
Carbon dioxide for insufflation
Heliox mixture
Helium for heliox
Entonox (N2O/O2)
Suction
questions.explanation: The DISS chart on slide 6 lists oxygen, nitrous oxide, air, suction, and WAGD, each with its own connector. CO2, helium, and Entonox appear on the cylinder (PISS) chart, not the DISS pipeline chart.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 6 (PDF p. 3)

questions.stem: Why must each Thorpe tube flowmeter be calibrated for one specific gas?
options: Each gas has a different critical temperature in the tube
The float material reacts differently with each gas
Gases differ in density and viscosity, which change the float position
Each gas arrives at a different pipeline supply pressure
questions.explanation: Float height depends on the pressure needed to support it: viscosity governs at low (laminar) flows and density at high (turbulent) flows. Because gases differ in these properties, each flowmeter is gas-specific, though gases with similar densities would read similarly.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 12 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: A brand-new breathing circuit won't pass gas during the machine check; pressure builds with the flush and nothing reaches the mask. What should be checked first?
options: Leftover plastic wrapping on a connector
The O2 cylinder pressure
The vaporizer filler cap
The scavenger vacuum setting
questions.explanation: Occlusions are usually from bent tubing, misconnections, or plastic wrapping not fully removed from breathing system components. Instructor note: watch for unremoved plastic wrapping; the machine check will catch it.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 22 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which fire preparation step is typically done during the surgical time-out?
options: Testing the ESU on a sponge
Pointing out the fire extinguisher location
Turning off room medical gases
Performing a full fire drill
questions.explanation: During time-out, staff typically point out the fire extinguisher location, and some teams confirm bovie use, pad placement, and fire-risk precautions out loud. Preparation also includes training, drills, and assigning each person a task.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 34 (PDF p. 17)

questions.stem: Besides adequate fresh gas flow, what design requirement does the lecture give for the Mapleson A tubing?
options: Fitted with a unidirectional valve at the patient end
Short enough that the bag attaches right at the mask
Long enough that exhaled CO2 doesn't reach the reservoir bag
Shorter than the patient's anatomic dead space volume
questions.explanation: For Mapleson A: FGF at least 0.7 x minute ventilation, AND the hose between the patient and reservoir bag must be long enough that exhaled CO2 doesn't reach the bag.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which are fire-prevention measures listed in the lecture? Select 3.
options: Tuck drapes tightly around the face during MAC
Use N2O in place of O2 to lower flammability
Configure drapes to avoid buildup of oxidizer
Moisten gauze and sponges near the ignition source
Let prep solutions pool so they stay moist
Avoid N2O
questions.explanation: Prevention: let flammable skin prep dry before draping, configure drapes to avoid oxidizer buildup, keep O2 as low as clinically possible, avoid N2O, notify the surgeon when oxidizer and ignition are close, and moisten gauze near the ignition source. N2O is an oxidizer, and tucking drapes traps O2.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 35 (PDF p. 18)

questions.stem: Some machines have an outlet check valve and a pressure relief valve near the common gas outlet. What do they protect?
options: The scavenger, from excessive suction at the interface
The patient's lungs, from O2 flush pressure surges
The hospital pipeline, from backflow of anesthetic gas
The vaporizers, from excess pressure during a downstream obstruction
questions.explanation: The check valve and pressure relief valve prevent buildup of excessive pressure within the vaporizers in the event of a downstream obstruction.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: During facial surgery under MAC, the patient has O2 by nasal cannula and the surgeon is about to use cautery near the face. What does the lecture emphasize?
options: Switch the cannula to N2O to lower the O2 concentration
Tuck the drapes tightly around the face to contain the O2
Keep FiO2 as low as tolerated and tell the surgeon where O2 flows
Increase O2 flow to create a protective O2 layer
questions.explanation: Be especially cautious with open O2 delivery near the airway: keep FiO2 as low as clinically possible, avoid N2O (also an oxidizer), configure drapes so oxidizer doesn't build up, and notify the surgeon when oxidizer and ignition source are close.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 35 (PDF p. 18)

questions.stem: Per the lecture audio, why can't anesthesia complications be analyzed as isolated OR events?
options: They can trace through pre-op, PACU, post-op, and the floor
They're never reported outside the operating room
Their causes are always found in the anesthesia equipment
They occur only during induction and emergence phases
questions.explanation: A complication often isn't isolated to the OR; it can trace through pre-op, PACU, post-op, and the floor. That, plus rarity and limited risk-management training, makes anesthesia risk harder to study.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 16 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: After a power-failure event, the department adds a battery-charge check to the daily machine checklist. Which risk management step is this?
options: Estimating likelihood
Defining potential problems
Monitoring
Applying solutions
questions.explanation: Risk management steps: define potential problems, estimate likelihood, weigh the benefits of expending resources, apply solutions, and monitor. Adding the battery check is the solution; tracking whether it prevents future problems would be monitoring.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 16, 25 (PDF p. 8, 13)

questions.stem: The ETT has been pulled and gases stopped during an airway fire. Which sequence of the NEXT steps matches the lecture?
options: Mask ventilate first, then remove burning material, then saline
Saline into the airway, remove burning material, mask ventilate, then assess
Bronchoscopy first, then pour saline, then mask ventilate
Reintubate right away, then pour saline, then mask ventilate
questions.explanation: After simultaneously removing the tube and stopping gases: pour saline into the airway, remove burning material, mask ventilate, assess for injury, consider bronchoscopy, and reintubate.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 36 (PDF p. 18)

questions.stem: Which are reported causes of total breathing-circuit OCCLUSION (as opposed to leaks)? Select 3.
options: A disposable swivel connector crack
A vaporizer filler cap left loose
Plastic wrapping left on a component
A freestanding PEEP valve in the inspiratory limb
An incorrectly connected humidifier
A loose ETT connection under the drapes
questions.explanation: Reported occlusion causes: filters in the circuit, incorrectly connected humidifiers, manufacturing defects, failure to remove plastic wrapping, and a freestanding PEEP valve placed in the inspiratory limb. Loose connections, cracked connectors, and loose filler caps cause leaks, not occlusion.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 22 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: In an OR with ungrounded (isolated) power, a staff member touches one energized conductor while standing on the floor. Why is macroshock less likely than it would be at home?
options: Isolated power converts the AC supply into safer DC
The ungrounded supply runs at a much lower voltage
The equipment's ground wire blocks the current path
No path to ground exists, so no current flows through them
questions.explanation: In the OR's ungrounded system, current is isolated from ground potential. Touching a single conductor doesn't complete a circuit through the body to ground, which is the added macroshock protection the lecture describes. At home, power is grounded, so the same contact can complete a circuit.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 29, 30 (PDF p. 15)

questions.stem: On a machine whose proportioning system links only O2 and N2O, flows are O2 1 L/min, N2O 3 L/min, and pure helium 2 L/min. What is the delivered FiO2?
options: About 17%
About 21%
About 25%
About 33%
questions.explanation: The proportioner is satisfied (O2 is 25% of O2 + N2O), but helium adds volume without O2: 1 L O2 in 6 L total is about 17%. This is the lecture's warning that helium with O2 plus added N2O can deliver less than 21%.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 14 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: For right shoulder surgery, the ESU return pad has been placed on the left calf and ECG pads on the right chest. What is the problem?
options: Nothing; the pad should always be as far from the site as possible
The ECG pads must be placed on the return pad
The pad on the left side will prevent the ESU from working
The current path is long and runs near the ECG; pad should be close to the site, ECG far
questions.explanation: Place the return plate as close as possible to the operative site and ECG pads as far away as feasible. A left calf pad for right shoulder surgery sends current across the body, and ECG pads near the site pick up interference.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: During MAC for a facial procedure, why does the lecture say to configure the drapes carefully?
options: To keep O2 from pooling under drapes near the ignition source
To keep ECG leads from dislodging under the drapes
To keep the patient warmer during the procedure
To let the ESU return pad sit close to the face
questions.explanation: Configure surgical drapes to minimize the buildup of oxidizer, and take extra care with open O2 delivery near the airway. O2 trapped under drapes creates an oxidizer-rich pocket right where cautery is used.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 35 (PDF p. 18)

questions.stem: Which hypoxemia hazards on slide 19 are NOT highlighted as usually caught on the machine check? Select 3.
options: Cylinder filled with hypoxic gas
Disconnected O2 hose at the wall
Crossed hospital pipelines
Liquid O2 reservoir filled with nitrogen
Breathing circuit leak at a connection
Empty O2 cylinder on the machine yoke
questions.explanation: Upstream supply problems and hypoxic gas inside a cylinder aren't highlighted; a machine check can't easily detect that a gas is the wrong gas. Empty cylinders, circuit leaks, and disconnected hoses are highlighted as usually caught on the check. That's why the O2 analyzer matters even after a clean check.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 19 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: The inspiratory unidirectional valve sticks open. What happens during exhalation?
options: Exhaled gas bypasses the absorber into the scavenger
The reservoir bag collapses completely
Exhaled gas flows back into the inspiratory limb and is rebreathed
Fresh gas is vented through the APL before reaching the patient
questions.explanation: Unidirectional valves keep gas moving one way around the circle. With the inspiratory valve incompetent, exhaled CO2-rich gas can move backward into the inspiratory limb and be inhaled with the next breath, a hypercarbia hazard listed on slide 20.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Whenever cautery is used, SpO2 drops briefly and the ECG shows a chaotic rhythm, both normalizing when cautery stops. Which statements are correct? Select 2.
options: The patient is having intermittent V-fib from ESU current
The patient is desaturating from ESU-induced shunting
ESU energy is interfering with the pulse oximeter
The return pad needs to move closer to the ECG pads
ESU energy is interfering with the ECG
The pulse oximeter probe should be placed on the return pad
questions.explanation: The Bovie's high-frequency energy interferes with the ECG, pulse oximeters, cardiac output computers, and pacemakers. Changes that appear only with cautery and resolve when it stops are interference. ESU frequencies don't cause V-fib, and the ECG belongs far from the pad.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: Two O2 cylinders on a double yoke are both left open, one at 2000 psig and one at 500 psig. Which statements are correct? Select 2.
options: The shared gauge can't show the two cylinder pressures separately
Transfilling only occurs with N2O cylinders
Gas can transfill from the higher- to the lower-pressure cylinder
The shared gauge shows the average of the two cylinders
The first-stage regulator stops transfilling
The yoke check valves keep the two pressures permanently separate
questions.explanation: The double hanger yoke allows transfilling, gas flowing from a higher- to a lower-pressure cylinder. On a two-cylinder system, the gauge location means individual cylinder pressures can't be differentiated. Open both and you lose track of your true reserve.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 7, 9 (PDF p. 4, 5)

questions.stem: A person with 1,000 ohms of resistance contacts a 120 V source. Standing in a saline puddle cuts resistance to 500 ohms. What happens to the current?
options: It doubles, from 120 mA to 240 mA
It halves, from 120 mA to 60 mA
It stays at 120 mA
It rises from 12 mA to 24 mA
questions.explanation: I = E / R. 120 / 1,000 = 0.12 A (120 mA); 120 / 500 = 0.24 A (240 mA). Halving resistance doubles current, which is why spilled fluids make the OR electrically hazardous.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 26, 30 (PDF p. 13, 15)

questions.stem: After a circuit is rebuilt, the reservoir bag sits between the patient and the expiratory valve. Which rule does this break, and what is the consequence?
options: The absorber must be on the bag side; compound A results
The APL must not sit between the patient and inspiratory valve; hypoxemia results
The bag must not sit between the patient and either valve; rebreathing results
The fresh gas inlet must not sit between the patient and expiratory valve; barotrauma results
questions.explanation: Three arrangements must be avoided to prevent rebreathing, including the reservoir bag between the patient and the inspiratory or expiratory valve. A bag in that position becomes a reservoir of exhaled gas.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: A fluid warmer plugged into the anesthesia machine's convenience outlet trips its circuit breaker. What is the likely effect?
options: The O2 fail-safe valve closes
The whole machine shuts down immediately
The machine switches to battery for the rest of the case
The outlet circuit loses power, while the machine's own supply is protected
questions.explanation: The machine has several circuit breakers, generally protecting separate circuits for the AC supply, the battery, and the convenience receptacles. A tripped outlet breaker cuts that circuit without taking down the workstation.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 25 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: A closed claim involves a patient harmed by a gas delivery problem. Based on the lecture, which contributing cause is most likely?
options: Hospital pipeline failure alone
Spontaneous failure of a well-maintained machine
Human error, often combined with other factors
Manufacturer design defect
questions.explanation: Most adverse events are multifactorial, and human error is responsible for the majority, often through failure to check equipment, unfamiliarity, haste, inattention, distraction, or fatigue.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 17, 18 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: If a certain AC current is enough to cause ventricular fibrillation, about how much DC would be needed to do the same?
options: About one-third as much
About the same amount
About three times as much
About ten times as much
questions.explanation: It takes approximately three times as much DC as AC to cause ventricular fibrillation. That still doesn't make DC harmless.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 27 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: An intubated, paralyzed patient needs transport. Why is a Mapleson B or C with controlled ventilation acceptable here when it would be poor for a spontaneously breathing patient?
options: Mapleson A can't be used with an ETT
With controlled ventilation, the patient doesn't do the extra work of breathing
B and C don't allow rebreathing during controlled ventilation
B and C need less fresh gas than a Mapleson A
questions.explanation: B and C always permit rebreathing, so hyperventilation with FGF of 1.5-2.5 x MV is needed. In a spontaneously breathing patient, that raises metabolic work; controlled ventilation doesn't create that problem because the patient isn't doing the work. Mapleson A is for spontaneous breathing.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which items does the lecture identify as FUEL in the OR? Select 3.
options: Room air
Tracheal tubes
Fiberoptic light cords
Nitrous oxide
Gel mattress pads
Facial or body hair
questions.explanation: Fuel includes paper drapes, gauze dressings, tracheal tubes, gel mattress pads, and facial or body hair. N2O and air are oxidizers, and fiberoptic light cord ends are ignition sources.
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 33 (PDF p. 17)

questions.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient with a minute ventilation of 8 L/min is transported on circuit 3 at 8 L/min fresh gas flow. Is that adequate?
options: No; circuit 3 needs about 12-20 L/min
Yes; it exceeds 0.7 x MV (5.6 L/min)
Yes; any FGF equal to MV prevents rebreathing
No; circuit 3 needs about 16-24 L/min
questions.explanation: Circuit 3 is the Mapleson C (fresh gas near the patient, no corrugated tubing), which always permits rebreathing and needs 1.5-2.5 x MV: 1.5 x 8 = 12 and 2.5 x 8 = 20 L/min. 0.7 x MV applies only to Mapleson A (circuit 1).
questions.citation: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)
